facts.statement: The type species Iguanodon bernissartensis lived during the Barremian age of the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early Cretaceous (Barremian)

facts.statement: The genus Iguanodon was described by Gideon Mantell in 1825.
facts.quote: authority: Mantell, 1825

facts.statement: Iguanodon bernissartensis is the type species of the genus Iguanodon.
facts.quote: type_species: Iguanodon bernissartensis

facts.statement: I. anglicus, described by Holl in 1829, is considered a nomen dubium, while I. galvensis was named by Verdú et al. in 2015.
facts.quote: subdivision: *†I. anglicusHoll, 1829 (nomen dubium) †I.? galvensisVerdú et al., 2015

facts.statement: Delapparentia turolensis, described by Ruiz-Omeñaca in 2011, is listed as a synonym of Iguanodon.
facts.quote: synonyms: *?Delapparentia turolensis Ruiz-Omeñaca, 2011

facts.statement: Iguanodon is a genus of iguanodontian dinosaurs named in 1825.
facts.quote: Iguanodon ( ; meaning 'iguana-tooth'), named in 1825, is a genus of iguanodontian dinosaur.

facts.statement: Many species historically classified in the genus Iguanodon date from the Late Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: While many species found worldwide have been classified in the genus Iguanodon, dating from the Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous

facts.statement: Iguanodon bernissartensis lived in Belgium, Germany, Spain, and possibly England between 126 and 122 million years ago during the Barremian to early Aptian ages.
facts.quote: Iguanodon bernissartensis, which lived during the Barremian to early Aptian ages of the Early Cretaceous in Belgium, Germany, Spain, and possibly England, between about 126 and 122 million years ago.

facts.statement: Iguanodon was a large, bulky herbivore reaching up to 9 to 11 meters in length and 4.5 metric tons in body mass.
facts.quote: Iguanodon was a large, bulky herbivore, measuring up to 9 - 11 m in length and 4.5 MT in body mass.

facts.statement: Iguanodon possessed large thumb spikes possibly used for defense and long prehensile fifth fingers used for foraging.
facts.quote: Distinctive features include large thumb spikes, which were possibly used for defense against predators, combined with long prehensile fifth fingers able to forage for food.

facts.statement: Gideon Mantell named the genus Iguanodon in 1825 based on fossil specimens found in England.
facts.quote: The genus was named in 1825 by English geologist Gideon Mantell, based on fossil specimens found in England

facts.statement: Iguanodon was the second dinosaur formally named based on fossil specimens, following Megalosaurus.
facts.quote: Iguanodon was the second type of dinosaur formally named based on fossil specimens, after Megalosaurus.

facts.statement: Iguanodon belongs to the larger group Iguanodontia, which also includes duck-billed hadrosaurs.
facts.quote: The genus Iguanodon belongs to the larger group Iguanodontia, along with the duck-billed hadrosaurs.

facts.statement: It is debated whether remains previously referred to as Iguanodon in England belong to I. bernissartensis or to other genera like Mantellisaurus, Barilium, and Hypselospinus.
facts.quote: In the early 21st century it became understood that the remains referred to as Iguanodon in England belonged to at least four different genera and species (possibly including I. bernissartensis) that were not closely related to each other, which were subsequently split off into Mantellisaurus, Barilium and Hypselospinus.

facts.statement: The originally described type species I. anglicus is now considered a nomen dubium and invalid.
facts.quote: It was also found that the originally described type species of Iguanodon, I. anglicus is now a nomen dubium, and not valid.

facts.statement: Numerous specimens, including nearly complete skeletons from two bone beds, have allowed researchers to form hypotheses about the feeding, movement, and social behavior of Iguanodon.
facts.quote: The numerous specimens of this genus, including nearly complete skeletons from two well-known bone beds, have allowed researchers to make informed hypotheses regarding many aspects of the living animal, including feeding, movement, and social behaviour.

facts.statement: A popular legend suggests Mary Ann Mantell discovered the first Iguanodon teeth in Tilgate Forest in 1822, though there is no evidence she accompanied her husband.
facts.quote: The story posits that Gideon Mantell's wife, Mary Ann, discovered the first teeth of an Iguanodon in the strata of Tilgate Forest in Whitemans Green, Sussex, England, in 1822 while her husband was visiting a patient.

facts.statement: Mantell's notebooks indicate he first acquired large fossil bones from the Whitemans Green quarry in 1820.
facts.quote: It is known from his notebooks that Mantell first acquired large fossil bones from the quarry at Whitemans Green in 1820.

facts.statement: Mantell initially interpreted the bones as belonging to a giant crocodile because theropod teeth were also found.
facts.quote: Because also theropod teeth were found, thus belonging to carnivores, he at first interpreted these bones, which he tried to combine into a partial skeleton, as those of a giant crocodile.

facts.statement: In 1821, Mantell noted the discovery of herbivorous teeth and considered the possibility of a large herbivorous reptile.
facts.quote: In 1821 Mantell mentioned the find of herbivorous teeth and began to consider the possibility that a large herbivorous reptile was present in the strata.

facts.statement: On June 23, 1823, Charles Lyell showed the teeth to Georges Cuvier in Paris, who initially dismissed them as rhinoceros teeth.
facts.quote: On 23 June 1823 Charles Lyell showed some to Georges Cuvier, during a soiree in Paris, but the famous French naturalist at once dismissed them as those of a rhinoceros.

facts.statement: Cuvier retracted his dismissal the next day, but Lyell only reported the initial dismissal to Mantell.
facts.quote: Though the very next day Cuvier retracted, Lyell reported only the dismissal to Mantell, who became rather diffident about the issue.

facts.statement: On March 6, 1824, William Buckland visited Mantell's collection and agreed the bones were from a giant saurian, though he denied it was a herbivore.
facts.quote: In 1824 Buckland described Megalosaurus and was on that occasion invited to visit Mantell's collection. Seeing the bones on 6 March he agreed that these were of some giant saurian—though still denying it was a herbivore.

facts.statement: In September 1824, Samuel Stutchbury recognized that the teeth resembled those of an iguana, but twenty times longer.
facts.quote: In September 1824 he visited the Royal College of Surgeons but at first failed to find comparable teeth. However, assistant-curator Samuel Stutchbury recognised that they resembled those of an iguana he had recently prepared, albeit twenty times longer.

facts.statement: Mantell named the animal Iguanodon, meaning 'iguana-tooth', based on the resemblance of the teeth to those of an iguana.
facts.quote: In recognition of the resemblance of the teeth to those of the iguana, Mantell decided to name his new animal Iguanodon or 'iguana-tooth', from iguana and the Greek word ὀδών (odon, odontos or 'tooth').

facts.statement: Based on isometric scaling, Mantell estimated the creature could be up to 18 meters long, longer than Megalosaurus.
facts.quote: Based on isometric scaling, he estimated that the creature might have been up to 18 m long, more than the 12 m length of Megalosaurus.

facts.statement: Friedrich Holl supplied the specific name I. anglicum in 1829, which was later emended to I. anglicus.
facts.quote: He neglected to add a specific name to form a proper binomial, but one was supplied in 1829 by Friedrich Holl: I. anglicum, which was later emended to I. anglicus.

facts.statement: Mantell formally published his findings on February 10, 1825, by presenting a paper to the Royal Society of London.
facts.quote: Mantell formally published his findings on 10 February 1825, when he presented a paper on the remains to the Royal Society of London.

facts.statement: A more complete specimen was discovered in a quarry in Maidstone, Kent, in 1834 and acquired by Mantell.
facts.quote: A more complete specimen of a similar animal was discovered in a quarry in Maidstone, Kent, in 1834 (lower Lower Greensand Formation), which Mantell soon acquired.

facts.statement: The Maidstone slab was used in early reconstructions, leading Mantell to mistakenly place a horn on the nose.
facts.quote: The Maidstone slab (NHMUK PV OR 3791) was used in the first skeletal reconstructions and artistic renderings of Iguanodon, but due to its incompleteness, Mantell made some mistakes, the most famous of which was the placement of what he thought was a horn on the nose.

facts.statement: Later discoveries revealed that the structure Mantell thought was a nose horn was actually a modified thumb.
facts.quote: The discovery of much better specimens in later years revealed that the horn was actually a modified thumb.

facts.statement: The Maidstone skeleton is currently displayed at the Natural History Museum in London.
facts.quote: Still encased in rock, the Maidstone skeleton is currently displayed at the Natural History Museum in London.

facts.statement: The Maidstone specimen was linked to I. mantelli, named in 1832, but it comes from a different geological formation than the original material.
facts.quote: This specimen has become linked with the name I. mantelli, a species named in 1832 by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer in place of I. anglicus, but it actually comes from a different formation than the original I. mantelli/I. anglicus material.

facts.statement: The Maidstone specimen, labelled NHMUK 3741, was subsequently excluded from the genus Iguanodon.
facts.quote: The Maidstone specimen, also known as Gideon Mantell's "Mantel-piece", and formally labelled NHMUK 3741 was subsequently excluded from Iguanodon.

facts.statement: The Maidstone specimen is generally considered a specimen of Mantellisaurus, though it has been proposed as the holotype of Mantellodon carpenteri by Paul in 2012.
facts.quote: It is classified as cf. Mantellisaurus by McDonald (2012); as cf. Mantellisaurus atherfieldensis by Norman (2012); and made the holotype of a separate species Mantellodon carpenteri by Paul (2012), but this is considered dubious and it is generally considered a specimen of Mantellisaurus.

facts.statement: Gideon Mantell realized in 1849 that Iguanodon had slender forelimbs rather than being heavy, pachyderm-like animals.
facts.quote: In 1849, a few years before his death in 1852, Mantell realised that iguanodonts were not heavy, pachyderm-like animals, as Owen was putting forward, but had slender forelimbs.

facts.statement: The largest known find of Iguanodon remains occurred on 28 February 1878 in a coal mine at Bernissart, Belgium, at a depth of 322 meters.
facts.quote: The largest find of Iguanodon remains to that date occurred on 28 February 1878 in a coal mine at Bernissart in Belgium, at a depth of 322 m

facts.statement: At least 38 Iguanodon individuals were uncovered at the Bernissart mine, most of which were adults.
facts.quote: At least 38 Iguanodon individuals were uncovered, most of which were adults.

facts.statement: In 1882, the holotype specimen of Iguanodon bernissartensis became one of the first dinosaur skeletons ever mounted for display.
facts.quote: In 1882, the holotype specimen of I. bernissartensis became one of the first ever dinosaur skeletons mounted for display.

facts.statement: The Bernissart Iguanodon skeletons first opened for public viewing in July 1883 in the inner courtyard of the Palace of Charles of Lorraine.
facts.quote: This specimen, along with several others, first opened for public viewing in an inner courtyard of the palace in July 1883.

facts.statement: In 1891, the Bernissart Iguanodon skeletons were moved to the Royal Museum of Natural History in Brussels, where they remain on display.
facts.quote: In 1891 they were moved to the Royal Museum of Natural History, where they are still on display

facts.statement: Most of the Bernissart remains were referred to the new species Iguanodon bernissartensis, which was larger and more robust than previously known English remains.
facts.quote: Most of the remains were referred to a new species, I. bernissartensis, a larger and much more robust animal than the English remains had yet revealed.

facts.statement: Specimen IRSNB 1551 was initially referred to Iguanodon mantelli but is now classified as Mantellisaurus atherfieldensis.
facts.quote: One specimen, IRSNB 1551, was at first referred to the nebulous, gracile I. mantelli, but is currently referred to Mantellisaurus atherfieldensis.

facts.statement: Fossils found alongside the Iguanodon skeletons included plants, fish, and other reptiles such as the crocodyliform Bernissartia.
facts.quote: Found with the dinosaur skeletons were the remains of plants, fish, and other reptiles, including the crocodyliform Bernissartia.

facts.statement: Between December 1935 and August 1936, Brussels museum staff treated the Bernissart fossils with alcohol, arsenic, and 390 kilograms of shellac to address pyrite disease.
facts.quote: From December 1935 to August 1936 the staff at the museum in Brussels treated the problem with a combination of alcohol, arsenic, and 390 kilograms of shellac.

facts.statement: The Bernissart fossils underwent a third conservation round from 2003 to May 2007, during which old treatments were removed and replaced with polyvinyl acetate, cyanoacrylate, and epoxy glues.
facts.quote: The fossils entered a third round of conservation from 2003 until May 2007, when the shellac, hide glue and gelatine were removed and impregnated with polyvinyl acetate and cyanoacrylate and epoxy glues.

facts.statement: The species Iguanodon atherfieldensis was named in 1925 by R. W. Hooley based on a specimen from Atherfield Point on the Isle of Wight.
facts.quote: A new species that would become the subject of much study and taxonomic controversy, I. atherfieldensis, was named in 1925 by R. W. Hooley, for a specimen collected at Atherfield Point on the Isle of Wight.

facts.statement: A find in Nehden, Germany, included at least 15 individuals ranging from 2 to 8 meters in length, comprising both Mantellisaurus and Iguanodon bernissartensis.
facts.quote: At least 15 individuals, from 2 to 8 m long, have been found here, most of the individuals belong to the related Mantellisaurus (described as I. atherfieldensis, at that time believed to be another species of Iguanodon). but some are of I. bernissartensis.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests Iguanodon lived in groups, as a find in Germany indicates the animals were killed together by flash floods.
facts.quote: a further find of numerous disarticulated Iguanodon bones in Nehden, Nordrhein-Westphalen, Germany, has provided evidence for gregariousness in this genus, as the animals in this areally restricted find appear to have been killed by flash floods.

facts.statement: Research indicates that Iguanodon had a straight tail and back, walking with its body held horizontally, rather than the bent tail previously reconstructed.
facts.quote: In fact, to get the bend in the tail for a more wallaby or kangaroo-like posture, the tail would have had to be broken.

facts.statement: Louis Dollo proposed that Iguanodon should be modeled after a cassowary or wallaby with the thumb spike on the thumb rather than the nose, a view that later prevailed but was eventually discounted.
facts.quote: Dollo's specimens allowed him to show that Owen's prehistoric pachyderms were not correct for Iguanodon. He instead modelled the skeletal mounts after the cassowary and wallaby, and put the spike that had been on the nose firmly on the thumb.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Dollo's reconstruction of Iguanodon was correct, specifically regarding the bend he introduced into the tail which contradicted fossil evidence.
facts.quote: A major flaw with Dollo's reconstruction was the bend he introduced into the tail.

facts.statement: In 2010, David Norman split the Valanginian species I. dawsoni and I. fittoni into the genera Barilium and Hypselospinus.
facts.quote: In 2010, David Norman split the Valanginian species I. dawsoni and I. fittoni into Barilium and Hypselospinus respectively.

facts.statement: In 2011, the genus Delapparentia was named for a Spanish specimen originally thought to belong to I. bernissartensis.
facts.quote: In 2011, a new genus Delapparentia was named for a specimen in Spain that was originally thought to belong to I. bernissartensis.

facts.statement: Iguanodon were bulky herbivores capable of shifting between bipedal and quadrupedal locomotion.
facts.quote: Iguanodon were bulky herbivores that could shift from bipedality to quadrupedality.

facts.statement: While Gregory S. Paul suggested an average body mass of 3.08 metric tons, 3D modeling suggests an average I. bernissartensis close to 8 meters long weighs about 3.8 metric tons.
facts.quote: Although Gregory S. Paul suggested a body mass of 3.08 MT on average, constructing a 3D mathematical model and employing allometry-based estimate suggests an I. bernissartensis close to 8 m long (smaller than average) weighs close to 3.8 MT in body mass.

facts.statement: The arms of I. bernissartensis were long, up to 75% the length of the legs, with robust, inflexible hands where the three central fingers could bear weight.
facts.quote: The arms of I. bernissartensis were long (up to 75% the length of the legs) and robust, with rather inflexible hands built so that the three central fingers could bear weight.

facts.statement: The thumbs of Iguanodon were conical spikes that protruded away from the three main digits.
facts.quote: The thumbs were conical spikes that stuck out away from the three main digits.

facts.statement: The little finger was elongated and dextrous, likely used for manipulating objects.
facts.quote: The little finger was elongated and dextrous, and could have been used to manipulate objects.

facts.statement: The phalangeal formula of Iguanodon is 2-3-3-2-4, indicating the number of bones in each finger sequence.
facts.quote: The phalangeal formula is 2-3-3-2-4, meaning that the innermost finger (phalange) has two bones, the next has three, etc.

facts.statement: Iguanodon had large, tall, narrow skulls with toothless keratin-covered beaks and large, closely packed teeth resembling those of iguanas.
facts.quote: These animals had large, tall but narrow skulls, with toothless beaks probably covered with keratin, and teeth like those of iguanas, as the name suggests, but much larger and more closely packed.

facts.statement: Due to deeply inset tooth rows and other anatomical details, it is believed that Iguanodon had a cheek-like structure to retain food in the mouth.
facts.quote: Because the tooth rows are deeply inset from the outside of the jaws, and because of other anatomical details, it is believed that, as with most other ornithischians, Iguanodon had some sort of cheek-like structure, muscular or non-muscular, to retain food in the mouth.

facts.statement: In older sources, Iguanodontidae was treated as a distinct family that served as a wastebasket taxon for ornithopods that were neither hypsilophodontids nor hadrosaurids.
facts.quote: In older sources, Iguanodontidae was shown as a distinct family. This family traditionally has been something of a wastebasket taxon, including ornithopods that were neither hypsilophodontids or hadrosaurids.

facts.statement: Cladistic analyses showed that traditionally construed Iguanodontidae was paraphyletic, with its members falling at different points relative to hadrosaurs rather than forming a single distinct clade.
facts.quote: With the advent of cladistic analyses, Iguanodontidae as traditionally construed was shown to be paraphyletic, and these animals are recognised to fall at different points in relation to hadrosaurs on a cladogram, instead of in a single distinct clade.

facts.statement: In modern classification, the concept of Iguanodontidae includes only the genus Iguanodon.
facts.quote: Essentially, the modern concept of Iguanodontidae currently includes only Iguanodon.

facts.statement: Jack Horner once proposed that hadrosaurids formed two distinct groups with Iguanodon on the line to flat-headed hadrosaurines and Ouranosaurus on the line to crested lambeosaurines, but this proposal was rejected.
facts.quote: At one point, Jack Horner suggested, based mostly on skull features, that hadrosaurids actually formed two more distantly related groups, with Iguanodon on the line to the flat-headed hadrosaurines, and Ouranosaurus on the line to the crested lambeosaurines, but his proposal has been rejected.

facts.statement: A 2026 study questioned the assignment of British iguanodontian material to I. bernissartensis, arguing it had been used as a wastebasket taxon.
facts.quote: While a large amount of iguanodontian material from Britain has been referred to I. bernissartensis by late 20th and early 21st century researchers and in museum catalogues, generally based on their comparative robustness compared to material referred to Mantellisaurus (formerly "I." atherfieldensis), a 2026 study questioned this, arguing that I. bernissartensis had been used as a wastebasket taxon.

facts.statement: Researchers noted the high diversity of British Early Cretaceous iguanodontians and the lack of a proper formal diagnosis for I. bernissartensis, leaving its presence in Britain in need of reassessment.
facts.quote: They noted the high diversity of iguanodontians described in the 21st century from the British Early Cretaceous broadly contemporaneous with Belgian I. bernissartensis, including (in addition to the aforementioned Mantellisaurus) Brighstoneus, Comptonatus, Istiorachis and the newly described Paludohadros, and that a proper formal diagnosis that makes clear what distinguishes I. bernissartensis from other iguanodontians is lacking, thus leaving the presence of I. bernissartensis in Britain in need of reassessment.

facts.statement: Many species have historically been assigned to the genus Iguanodon.
facts.quote: numerous species have been assigned to it

facts.statement: The International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature officially changed the type species of Iguanodon to I. bernissartensis in March 2000.
facts.quote: In March 2000, the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature changed the type species to the much better known I. bernissartensis

facts.statement: The original Iguanodon tooth used as the lectotype is held at the Te Papa Tongarewa museum in Wellington, New Zealand.
facts.quote: The original Iguanodon tooth is held at Te Papa Tongarewa, the national museum of New Zealand in Wellington

facts.statement: Currently, only one species assigned to Iguanodon is considered valid by many researchers.
facts.quote: Only one species assigned to Iguanodon is still considered to be valid

facts.statement: Iguanodon bernissartensis, described by George Albert Boulenger in 1881, serves as the type species for the genus.
facts.quote: I. bernissartensis, described by George Albert Boulenger in 1881, is the type species for the genus

facts.statement: Iguanodon seelyi, described by John Hulke in 1882, has been synonymized with I. bernissartensis, though this is not universally accepted.
facts.quote: I. seelyi (also incorrectly spelled I. seeleyi), described by John Hulke in 1882, has also been synonymised with Iguanodon bernissartensis

facts.statement: The genus Iguanodon was established by Gideon Mantell in 1825.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Mantell, 1825

facts.statement: Iguanodon bernissartensis is the current type species of the genus Iguanodon.
facts.quote: type_species: Iguanodon bernissartensis

facts.statement: Iguanodon lived during the early Early Cretaceous period, between 126 and 120 million years ago (Barremian to Aptian stages).
facts.quote: que vivieron a principios del período Cretácico Inferior, entre 126 a 120 millones de años, entre el Barremiense y el Aptiense

facts.statement: Iguanodon fossils have been found in what is now Europe.
facts.quote: en lo que hoy es Europa

facts.statement: Iguanodon were large and robust herbivores.
facts.quote: Fueron herbívoros grandes y robustos

facts.statement: A main characteristic of Iguanodon is its large thumb claws.
facts.quote: La principal característica de Iguanodon son sus grandes garras en los pulgares

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the large thumb claws of Iguanodon may have been used to defend against predators.
facts.quote: que fueron utilizados posiblemente para defenderse de los depredadores

facts.statement: Iguanodon possessed long, grasping fifth toes capable of searching for food.
facts.quote: combinadas con los quintos dedos prensiles largos capaces de buscar comida

facts.statement: Iguanodon was a robust herbivore capable of alternating between bipedal and quadrupedal locomotion.
facts.quote: Iguanodon fue un robusto herbívoro que podía alternar entre las marchas bípeda y cuadrúpeda

facts.statement: Adults of the best-known species, I. bernissartensis, are estimated to have weighed an average of 3 tonnes.
facts.quote: Se ha estimado que los adultos de la especie mejor conocida, I. bernissartensis, pesaban un promedio de 3 toneladas

facts.statement: Adult I. bernissartensis measured approximately 10 meters in length, reaching up to 13 meters in some cases.
facts.quote: y medían cerca de 10 metros de largo, pudiendo alcanzar en algunos casos los 13 metros

facts.statement: The spine and tail of Iguanodon were reinforced and stiffened by cylindrical ossified tendons.
facts.quote: La espina dorsal y la cola estaban reforzadas y rigificadas por tendones osificados cilíndricos

facts.statement: It is debated whether I. bernissartensis includes the Mongolian species I. orientalis, a view suggested by David Norman but not followed by others.
facts.quote: David Norman has suggested that I. bernissartensis includes the dubious Mongolian I. orientalis (see also below), but this has not been followed by other researchers

facts.statement: A 2017 study noted that the differences in neural spine height between Delapparentia turolensis and I. bernissartensis fall within the range of individual variation.
facts.quote: However, a 2017 study noted that this is easily within the range of individual variation

facts.statement: Iguanodon had a large, high, but narrow skull with a toothless beak likely covered in keratin.
facts.quote: Este género tenía un cráneo grande, alto pero estrecho, con un desdentado pico cubierto probablemente con queratina

facts.statement: Iguanodon possessed a robust chewing apparatus with dentition typical of a herbivorous reptile.
facts.quote: Iguanodon poseía un robusto aparato masticador, dotado con la dentición típica de un reptil herbívoro

facts.statement: Iguanodon had a single replacement tooth for each tooth in use.
facts.quote: Iguanodon tenía un único diente de reemplazo por cada pieza dentaria en uso

facts.statement: Iguanodon had 29 teeth in each upper jaw and 25 teeth in each lower jaw.
facts.quote: Poseían 29 dientes en cada maxilar, 58 dientes superiores, y 25 en cada dentario, 50 dientes inferiores

facts.statement: Iguanodon had powerful legs that were not suited for running and three toes on each foot.
facts.quote: Las piernas eran poderosas, pero no aptas para la carrera, y tenían tres dedos en cada pie

facts.statement: In I. bernissartensis, the arms were long, reaching up to 75% of the leg length, and robust.
facts.quote: Los brazos eran largos, hasta 75% de la longitud de las piernas en I. bernissartensis y robustos

facts.statement: The little finger (digit V) was long and flexible, likely used for manipulating objects and aiding in food collection.
facts.quote: El dedo meñique, el dedo V, era alargado y flexible, y habría podido ser utilizado para manipular objetos y de ayuda en la recolección del alimento

facts.statement: A defining feature of Iguanodon is a large thumb with a second phalanx forming a large, well-developed conical claw likely covered in thick keratin.
facts.quote: Una de las características de Iguanodon es el gran dedo pulgar, dedo I o pollex, cuya segunda falange formaba gran una garra cónica, muy desarrollada y probablemente dotada con una gruesa cubierta córnea

facts.statement: The thumbs pointed outward, perpendicular to the three central fingers.
facts.quote: Los pulgares estaban dirigidos hacia fuera, perpendiculares a los tres dedos centrales

facts.statement: The function of the thumb claw is debated; it is traditionally viewed as a defensive weapon but may also have been used to crack seeds and fruits.
facts.quote: Este pulgar es tradicionalmente explicado como un elemento defensivo contra los predadores o contra otros Iguanodon, aunque pudo usarlo también para partir semillas y frutas

facts.statement: It has been hypothesized that the thumb claw was associated with a venom gland, but this hypothesis is disputed due to a lack of anatomical evidence.
facts.quote: Se ha propuesto también la posibilidad de que la garra estuviera asociada a una glándula venenosa, pero la hipótesis está en entredicho

facts.statement: In initial reconstructions, Mantell mistakenly identified the last phalanx of the thumb as a horn placed on the nose.
facts.quote: En las reconstrucciones iniciales Mantell confundió la última falange del pulgar con un cuerno que ubicó sobre la nariz

facts.statement: Iguanodon belongs to the parent group Ankylopollexia.
facts.quote: Parent group: Ankylopollexia

facts.statement: Iguanodon is classified in the class Ornithischia.
facts.quote: Class: Ornithischia

facts.statement: Iguanodon lived from the Kimmeridgian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 154.8 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Kimmeridgian to Maastrichtian (154.8 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Verdú et al. (2026) provided new information on the variability of Iguanodon cranial morphology.
facts.quote: New information on variability of cranial morphology of Iguanodon is provided by Verdú et al. (2026)

rejected.statement: Iguanodon, along with Megalosaurus and Hylaeosaurus, was one of the three genera originally used to define the group Dinosauria.
rejected.quote: Together with Megalosaurus and Hylaeosaurus, it was one of the three genera originally used to define Dinosauria.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'was one of the three genera originally used'

rejected.statement: New, more complete remains of Iguanodon were discovered in Belgium in 1878 and studied by Louis Dollo.
rejected.quote: In 1878, new, far more complete remains of Iguanodon were discovered in Belgium and studied by Louis Dollo.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'more complete remains of Iguanodon were discovered in'

rejected.statement: The remains discovered in Belgium in 1878 were assigned to the new species Iguanodon bernissartensis.
